doc.title: Wendy Oxenhorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 22, 2026

title: Going national, Katrina and growth of the Foundation
summary: The Foundation went national, ran a doctors' network, helped musicians after Katrina, and grew to 70 million dollars and 8,000 cases a year.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Yes. Yeah. The foundation, you know I basically have turned into – within two years we were national. I was helping musicians not just in New York but finding out about someone in another state, finding out they needed a doctor, they had no health insurance, finding out who the specialist was in that state and ask them would you just take on this one musician for free, could you please. And we’d get this doctors’ network going and our blessed saints, the Englewood Hospital in Jersey was taking musicians for free because of a relationship with Dizzy Gillespie and then something Jimmy Owens did, so they were treating musicians for free but it became a big deal, like to the tune of eight million dollars. It just started growing. And then when Katrina happened and I went to New Orleans I started discovering all the musicians that lost their homes, lost everything. We started doing that and I was able to now start to hire people because we needed it. We had I think a thousand musicians that year and it was nothing less than a 20-hour day. That was another thing. You don’t sleep or do much of anything else in moments like that. But that’s what put us on the map. And then I got this amazing St. Agnes, you know, and I didn’t name the man who gave us the original 15 thousand, it was Jarrett Lillen, who I made our president one day when he was not at the board meeting. I invited him onto the board and then in his absence we voted him – I asked for everyone to vote him on as president. That’s how we did things back then. But fast forward to like I think

generated 70 million dollars later, and helping about 8,000 cases a year, and we would help. Like a case could be sometimes two or three for one musician because there was always such a need. There was the short term need of like getting the rent paid so they don’t get evicted and lose their rent-controlled apartment, and then there was the long term need, finding out they needed to have work in order to keep paying the rent. So I had developed the Jazz in the Schools program which ended up across the country helping hundreds of elders. You know? And that’s how we got the New Orleans musicians back on their feet in the states they were displaced to. Anyway it’s all too much to talk about but it really became wonderful. It became a love-oiled machine. And it was really built on love but you know the people I put in power on our board, Dick Parsons and Jarrett Lillen and my mentee Joe Petrucelli – Jarrett Lillen really felt that you have to take it to the next level and you will want it to go way beyond you and you want it to live beyond you, Wendy. So he suggested that you know I kind of hand it over to them, that they can take it to that next level. I thought we were doing pretty good, but you know it’s funny my – the thing that I love to do most is, and I learned this with Street News too with the homeless, when you keep something contained in a smaller fashion it’s wonderful to help more people. It’s fantastic. And I’m thrilled that that’s the direction that it’s going in. But when I started it that going to someone’s home, that having the time, having 45 minutes to speak to someone on the phone. I used to call four musicians a night when my kids would go to sleep, just to keep in touch. Just to keep that sense of family going after the emergency so they wouldn’t need to have an emergency. Plus you become friends and family with them. And plus they give you your energy back because they’re all so fascinating. We would have deep, fabulous conversations but there was this bond and this soul connection. And that’s what I found, that you know when something gets too big, just like Street News, it no longer is what I – I could no longer be the best person I can be for it. You know? I can get it there, but then it’s time really to hand it over. They were right. It’s time to hand it over. You know? And what I’m doing now is beautiful if it’s okay to mention?
